Cholesterol Metabolism Pathways: Synthesis, Uptake, Esterification, and Efflux in Cellular Homeostasis

Cholesterol Metabolism Pathways: Synthesis, Uptake, Esterification, and Efflux in Cellular Homeostasis. Cellular cholesterol homeostasis is maintained through coordinated de novo synthesis, lipoprotein uptake, intracellular trafficking, esterification, and efflux. De novo synthesis proceeds from acetyl-CoA through the mevalonate pathway (including HMG-CoA reductase as a key rate-limiting enzyme) to generate sterol intermediates and cholesterol, while also producing non-sterol isoprenoids (for example, FPP/GGPP), dolichol, and coenzyme Q. Extracellular cholesterol is acquired mainly through LDL–LDLR-mediated endocytosis. In endosomes and lysosomes, cholesteryl esters are hydrolyzed to free cholesterol, which is exported by the NPC2/NPC1 system and redistributed to cellular membranes and organelles; PCSK9 promotes LDLR lysosomal degradation and thereby limits LDL uptake. Excess free cholesterol can be esterified by SOAT1/2 (ACAT1/2) and stored in lipid droplets. Cholesterol efflux is mediated by ATP-binding cassette transporters, including ABCA1/ABCG1, whereas ABCG5/ABCG8 support intestinal and hepatobiliary sterol secretion. Together, these pathways preserve membrane integrity, signaling competence, and metabolic homeostasis
